title: Place n queens on an n-by-n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and count or list all valid placements, using backtracking.
shortTitle: Solve the N-Queens Problem (Backtracking with Constraint Pruning)

s1_definition.profdef: The N-Queens problem places n chess queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal. Backtracking solves it row by row: in each row you try every column, skip columns that conflict with an already-placed queen, place a queen in a safe column, recurse to the next row, then remove it to try alternatives. Constraint sets for occupied columns and both diagonal directions make the safety check constant time per cell.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must assign n critical daily jobs to n time slots on n servers so that no two jobs clash on the same resource line, where the clash rules mirror a queen's reach: same column, or either diagonal. A scheduler fills one job per row. For each row she tries each column, but skips any column or diagonal already claimed by an earlier job. When she finds a free spot she places the job and moves to the next row; if a row has no free spot she backs up and reshuffles the previous placement. Every complete fill with no clashes is one valid schedule.
s1_definition.oneliner: Place one queen per row in a non-conflicting column, tracking used columns and both diagonals, and backtrack when a row has no safe cell.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The N-Queens problem places n chess queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal. Backtracking solves it row by row: in each row you try every column, skip columns that conflict with an already-placed queen, place a queen in a safe column, recurse to the next row, then remove it to try alternatives. Constraint sets for occupied columns and both diagonal directions make the safety check constant time per cell.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must assign n critical daily jobs to n time slots on n servers so that no two jobs clash on the same resource line, where the clash rules mirror a queen's reach: same column, or either diagonal. A scheduler fills one job per row. For each row she tries each column, but skips any column or diagonal already claimed by an earlier job. When she finds a free spot she places the job and moves to the next row; if a row has no free spot she backs up and reshuffles the previous placement. Every complete fill with no clashes is one valid schedule.

**One line to remember:** Place one queen per row in a non-conflicting column, tracking used columns and both diagonals, and backtrack when a row has no safe cell.

sections.s2_technical:
The key realisation that shrinks the search is that exactly one queen goes in each row, so you never need to decide "how many queens in this row"; you just pick a column for the current row and move on. That turns the problem into choosing a column per row, which is at most n choices per row.

The safety test must be constant time to keep the search fast, so you maintain three sets. One set of used columns catches same-column conflicts. The two diagonal directions are captured by arithmetic: cells on the same "down-right" diagonal share the value row minus column, and cells on the same "down-left" diagonal share row plus column. So you keep a set of occupied row-minus-column values and a set of occupied row-plus-column values. A cell at row r and column c is safe exactly when its column, its r minus c, and its r plus c are all absent from the three sets. Placing a queen adds those three keys; backtracking removes them.

The recursion fills rows in order. At the base case, when the row index equals n, every row has a safe queen, so you have a complete solution and you record or count it. Otherwise you loop over columns, skip unsafe ones, place by adding the three constraint keys and recording the column, recurse into the next row, then undo all of that. This add-recurse-undo over the three sets is the backtracking rhythm, and the constraint sets are what make it efficient rather than re-scanning the board.

A senior-level nuance is the complexity and the symmetry optimisations. The naive bound is n to the n, but the per-row single-queen rule and the constant-time pruning cut this dramatically, though it remains super-polynomial. You can nearly halve the work by only trying the first half of columns in the first row and mirroring, and a famous bit-manipulation version represents the three constraint sets as bitmasks, using bitwise operations to find free columns in a few instructions. N-Queens is the textbook demonstration of constraint-satisfaction backtracking, the same paradigm behind Sudoku solvers and general CSP engines.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a constraint scheduler that must assign one critical job per time row to a server column such that conflicting resource lines, modelled like a queen's row, column, and diagonal reach, are never shared. Counting the valid assignments mirrors counting N-Queens solutions. This is exactly constraint-satisfaction backtracking.

Problem 2 — The conflict check happens an enormous number of times, so it must be constant time, otherwise the scheduler is too slow. Tracking used columns and both diagonal directions in sets gives a constant-time safety test and lets us prune impossible branches immediately.

In our mini-project we build a `QueenScheduler` that counts all valid n-queens placements using backtracking with three constraint sets. The demo solves the classic four-by-four board and logs the solution count.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a four-by-four board, counting valid placements.

Step 1: Enter row zero. Try column zero. It is safe since all sets are empty. Place a queen: add column zero, add diagonal keys zero and zero. Recurse into row one.

Step 2: In row one, column zero conflicts on the column set, column one conflicts on a diagonal with the row-zero queen, so the first safe column is two. Place it and recurse into row two.

Step 3: In row two, every column conflicts with the two queens already placed given the diagonals and columns used, so there is no safe cell. The recursion returns zero for this sub-branch, and we backtrack, removing the row-one queen and trying its next column, three. That leads to a dead end deeper down as well.

Step 4: We backtrack fully out of the row-zero-column-zero branch. Starting the row-zero queen at column one, however, leads to a complete safe filling of all four rows, which counts as one solution.

Step 5: Similarly, placing the row-zero queen at column two yields the mirror solution, the second valid placement, while columns zero and three for row zero lead to no complete solution.

Step 6: Summing the complete fills over all starting columns gives two valid four-queen placements, the known answer. The three constraint sets made each safety check constant time and pruned conflicting branches the instant they arose.

```
[2026-10-26 23:35:01] INFO    Valid 4-queen schedules: 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  n=4, fill one queen per row, prune by (col, row-col, row+col)

  row0: try col0 → place → row1...
         col0 blocked(col), col1 blocked(diag), col2 ok → row2 no safe → backtrack
  row0: col1 → leads to full valid board  → +1
  row0: col2 → mirror valid board         → +1
  row0: col0, col3 → dead ends            → +0

  total valid = 2
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — N-Queens (Constraint Backtracking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Constraint-satisfaction backtracking, one queen per row      │
  │  O(1) safety via column + two diagonal sets                   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: QueenScheduler only counts valid placements               │
  │  O: record boards instead of counting via same recursion      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            QueenScheduler             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - cols: Set<Integer>                 │  used columns
  │  - diagDownRight: Set<Integer>        │  row - col
  │  - diagDownLeft: Set<Integer>         │  row + col
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + countPlacements(n): int            │
  │  - backtrack(row, n): int             │  place/recurse/undo
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Safe(r,c): c ∉ cols ∧ r-c ∉ DR ∧ r+c ∉ DL

  ── State Diagram: Row fill ──────────────────────────────

  [row < n] ──safe col──→ place, recurse(row+1) ──→ undo
  [row == n] ──→ +1 solution (all rows filled)
  [no safe col] ──→ 0 for this branch (backtrack)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. countPlacements(n) → backtrack(0, n)
  2.   row==n → return 1
  3.   for col: if conflict skip; else place 3 keys; recurse; undo
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The N-Queens problem places n queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal, and I solve it with backtracking row by row. The single most important insight is that exactly one queen goes in each row, so I never decide how many queens a row holds; I just choose a safe column for the current row and recurse to the next. That reduces the problem to picking one column per row, at most n choices each.

To keep the safety check constant time, I maintain three sets. One set holds used columns, which catches same-column conflicts. The two diagonals are captured by arithmetic: all cells on one diagonal share the value row minus column, and all cells on the other share row plus column, so I keep a set of each. A cell is safe exactly when its column, its row-minus-column, and its row-plus-column are all absent from the three sets. Placing a queen adds those three keys, recursing fills the next row, and backtracking removes them. When the row index reaches n, every row is safely filled and I count one solution.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this pattern in a constraint scheduler that assigns one critical job per time row to a server column while avoiding shared resource lines modelled like a queen's reach. The conflict check runs an enormous number of times, so the constant-time set-based test was essential, and it let the scheduler prune impossible branches the instant a conflict appeared.

The senior-level point I make is that N-Queens is the textbook example of constraint-satisfaction backtracking, the same paradigm behind Sudoku solvers and general CSP engines. I note that while the per-row rule and constant-time pruning cut the search dramatically from the naive n-to-the-n, it is still super-polynomial, and I mention the optimisations I know: exploiting board symmetry to nearly halve the first row's choices, and the elegant bitmask version that stores the three constraint sets as integers and uses bitwise operations to find free columns in just a few instructions.
